page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.c6a.4xlarge is a compute-optimized virtual machine instance powered by the KVM hypervisor. It features 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 8 physical cores of an AMD EPYC 7H12 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.6 GHz. The instance is equipped with 32.0 GB of system memory, yielding a resource density of 2.0 GB per vCPU. It does not include local storage or a GPU, and it provides a baseline network bandwidth of 5 Gbps.

The underlying x86_64 architecture supports Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX), SHA extensions, and AES cryptography, though it lacks AVX-512 capabilities. In performance evaluations, the instance demonstrates a clear contrast between single-core and multi-core execution. While its single-core performance in stress-ng is positioned in the bottom 10%, its multi-core CPU performance and Geekbench multi-core scores fall within the middle 50% average. This indicates that workloads utilizing parallel execution will achieve more balanced throughput than those relying on single-threaded speed.

Memory bandwidth benchmarks reveal a tradeoff: small-block cached read operations perform at an average level, but large-block uncached reads and writes drop to the bottom 25%. Consequently, the instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for compute-bound tasks that fit within cache limits rather than memory-bandwidth-intensive applications. Appropriate workloads include multi-threaded compilation, static web serving, and database operations that align with its average multi-core and Redis SET performance.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.c6a.4xlarge is a compute-optimized instance featuring 16 dedicated vCPUs and 32.0 GB of RAM, powered by an AMD EPYC 7H12 processor at 2.6 GHz. Operating on the KVM hypervisor, this x86_64 server lacks local storage and GPUs, relying on a 5 Gbps baseline network. Performance benchmarks indicate a distinct tradeoff: single-core stress-ng performance is weak, ranking in the bottom 10%, whereas multi-core CPU, Geekbench, and PassMark scores consistently align with the middle 50% average. Memory bandwidth also drops for large, uncached blocks, though cached small-block reads remain average. This hardware profile is qualitatively cost-efficient for parallelized, compute-bound workloads such as multi-threaded software compilation, static web serving, and database operations that do not demand high single-thread performance or massive memory-to-CPU ratios.
